strengths: Simple yet effective approach using temporal distance prediction from passive videos; no action annotations required and rewards can be frozen during RL

Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 10 MetaWorld tasks with 8 random seeds, thorough ablation studies clearly showing contribution of each component, and comparison against 8 well-chosen baselines

Strong empirical results achieving 9/10 task success and outperforming baselines on both sample efficiency and final performance; VOC analysis (Figure 3) demonstrates good generalization to held-out expert videos
Demonstrates practical scalability benefits (frozen reward model requiring no online updates) over recent methods like PROGRESSOR and Rank2Reward
Cross-domain experiments showing ability to leverage human videos alongside minimal in-domain supervision, suggesting potential for real-world applicability
Thorough implementation details in appendix including hyperparameters, alternative design explorations, and clarification of experimental setup choices
weaknesses: Generalization mechanism to out-of-distribution behaviors not rigorously justified: while implicit negative sampling uses reversed frame pairs, the paper does not explain why training on expert-only data (even reversed) teaches the model to penalize realistic failures encountered during agent exploration; Section 4.3 proves temporal distance aligns with progress on expert trajectories but not on OOD agent behavior

Surprising and inadequately explained claim of surpassing ground-truth environment dense rewards on 9/10 tasks: lacks analysis of why this occurs, potential confounds in reward combination (Eq. 7), or whether diverse initialization disadvantages appearance-based rewards in ways specific to this setup

Real-world scalability claims overstated: cross-domain experiments involve only 3 tasks and 20 human videos per task, with modest improvements from adding human data; does not convincingly demonstrate ability to scale to truly diverse in-the-wild video sources as claimed in abstract

Significant acknowledged limitation inadequately investigated: paper admits failure on tasks with frequent back-and-forth motions but provides no evidence of which tasks fail, severity analysis, mechanistic explanation, or proposed solutions

Potentially unfair baseline comparisons: deliberate diverse initialization (Appendix A.4.2) is acknowledged to disadvantage OT/ADS by removing appearance shortcuts they rely on; unclear if comparison is fair or whether baselines could be adapted; VIP receives privileged goal frame information

Incomplete theoretical justification: derivation in Section 4.3 assumes expert optimality and γ≈1 but does not prove learned model will satisfy requirements; gap between why temporal distance equals progress in theory (on expert trajectories) versus why it generalizes to OOD agent behavior in practice

Limited conceptual novelty: temporal ordering as reward signal explored in prior work (TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR); implicit negatives inspired by GVL; two-hot discretization from other work; main contribution is combination of these existing ideas

Unspecified or missing design justifications: why K=20 bins specifically, sensitivity to λ parameter, value of α in experiments (stated in Eq. 7 but not in Tables 1-2), explanation for why discretization outperforms regression beyond empirical observation

Narrow experimental scope: all tasks are relatively short-horizon manipulation in simulation; limited to MetaWorld domain; unclear how method performs on longer-horizon, navigation, or substantially different task structures where temporal distance properties may differ

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 10 MetaWorld tasks with multiple baseline comparisons and thorough ablation studies demonstrating strong empirical results (9/10 task success)
Clear problem motivation and pragmatic approach using action-free passive videos without requiring manual reward engineering or action annotations
Well-motivated technical components (implicit negative sampling, exponentially weighted pair sampling, two-hot discretization) with clear ablations showing each component's contribution
Excellent presentation with informative visualizations (reward curves, VOC metrics, value-order correlation analysis) that provide good intuition for the approach
Demonstrated cross-domain generalization capability with human videos, showing practical potential for diverse video sources
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Predicting continuous temporal distances versus ranking (Rank2Reward) or relative positions (PROGRESSOR) is incremental; the paper lacks clear articulation of fundamental insights distinguishing it from recent prior work

Experimental setup has fairness concerns: (1) Deliberately uses 'diverse initialization' to intentionally hurt baseline methods OT/ADS that rely on appearance matching; (2) Provides goal frames to PROGRESSOR/VIP but TimeRewarder learns goals implicitly—asymmetric setup; these design choices bias results toward TimeRewarder

Weak theoretical justification: Section 4.3 is informal and hand-wavy; Equation 8 assumes normalized step cost without justification; assumes expert optimality without leveraging it; loose connection between theory assumptions (uniform costs, goal frames) and practice; doesn't explain why temporal distance should outperform alternatives

Limited evaluation scope: Only MetaWorld manipulation tasks with short horizons (~50-100 frames); cross-domain experiments restricted to 3 tasks with 20 human videos each; acknowledged failures on back-and-forth motions not investigated; no evaluation on long-horizon, non-manipulation, or other domains

Ablation studies test strawman alternatives (only-from-init, single-frame, order-prediction) that differ fundamentally from main approach rather than isolating temporal distance prediction contribution; missing ablations on continuous regression vs discretization and hyperparameter sensitivity

Critical missing analysis: No computational cost comparison; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (λ, K=20, α); limited evidence for out-of-distribution generalization beyond qualitative examples; no statistical significance testing despite showing error bars; no investigation of scalability with fewer demonstrations

Overselling and presentation issues: Claims like 'dramatically improves' and 'nearly perfect success' are not consistently supported; related work section doesn't clearly articulate differences from Rank2Reward/PROGRESSOR until deep reading; frozen reward model choice not justified against online refinement

Reproducibility concerns: Diverse initialization protocol makes baseline reproduction difficult; implementation details for some baselines unclear; experimental design choices (100 demos, specific initialization) not validated for robustness

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: frame-wise temporal distances in expert trajectories naturally encode task progress and serve as effective proxy rewards without requiring action annotations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation addressing four concrete research questions (Q1-Q4) with appropriate metrics (VOC, suboptimal detection, RL performance, cross-domain generalization)
Thorough ablation studies convincingly demonstrate the necessity of all three key components (implicit negative sampling, exponentially weighted sampling, two-hot discretization)
Strong empirical results: achieves 9/10 task success with only 200K interactions and outperforms both recent baselines and environment-provided dense rewards on most tasks
Practical advantages over prior work: frozen reward model eliminates online refinement needs and enables scaling to diverse video sources
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-structured narrative, thoughtful figures (especially Figures 3-4 showing reward quality comparisons), and comprehensive appendix
Provides theoretical grounding through connection to potential-based reward shaping (Section 4.3) and formal derivation relating temporal distance to task progress
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: restricted to 10 similar MetaWorld manipulation tasks; no evaluation on fundamentally different domains (navigation, locomotion, deformable objects) significantly limits generalization claims

Critical limitation underdeveloped: paper acknowledges failure on 'tasks with frequent back-and-forth motions' but provides no concrete examples, failure analysis, or solutions; mentioned solutions (hierarchical models) are speculative

Theoretical justification needs rigor: Section 4.3 relies on strong assumptions (expert optimality, uniform per-step cost) and doesn't formally prove generalization to out-of-distribution suboptimal states; connection between Equations 8-9 is hand-wavy
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: two-hot discretization K=20 appears arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; exponential weighting λ and reward weight α in Eq. 7 not thoroughly validated
Limited cross-domain experiments: only 3 tasks with 20 human videos each; single in-domain expert video per task is extreme constraint; missing extensive real-world evaluation

Implicit negative sampling not rigorously validated: paper doesn't analyze whether backward-ordered pairs always represent appropriate negatives; in some tasks reversing actions might represent valid alternative strategies
Statistical rigor concerns: claim of outperforming environment reward on 9/10 tasks (Figure 5) shows overlapping confidence intervals on several tasks, requiring significance testing

Scale and efficiency not analyzed: no computational cost analysis for reward model training; unclear how method scales with trajectory length and number of tasks; 200K interactions relatively small for claims of scalability

strengths: Clear, intuitive core idea: temporal ordering in videos encodes task progress, enabling self-supervised reward learning without action annotations
Strong empirical results: achieves 9/10 success on Meta-World with 200K frames, outperforming both recent baselines (VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR) and environment-designed dense rewards on 9/10 tasks

Thorough experimental evaluation: five well-structured research questions, meaningful ablations isolating each component, Value-Order Correlation validation on held-out trajectories, representation visualizations showing coherent structure

Elegant technical design: implicit negative sampling via reverse-ordered pairs prevents memorization while naturally encoding suboptimality; weighted pair sampling focuses on fine-grained progress; two-hot discretization ensures numerical stability
Cross-domain generalization: demonstrates ability to leverage heterogeneous video sources (human videos with different viewpoints) alongside limited in-domain data
Theoretical grounding: connects temporal distance to task progress via potential-based reward shaping and Bellman optimality equations
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap incompletely addressed: theoretical analysis assumes fully observable MDP, but visual RL is POMDP; visual aliasing counterexample (drawer-open) is presented but the proposed fix (observation histories) is never empirically validated or characterized for frequency in practice

Limited domain diversity: all 10 main experiments are Meta-World manipulation tasks; no evaluation on locomotion, navigation, or non-manipulation domains; generalization to tasks with different temporal structures unclear; ManiSkill3 (1 task) only in appendix

Non-standard experimental setup undermines reproducibility: Meta-World demonstrations use deliberately diverse initializations (A.5.2), differing from standard protocol; this explains poor OT/ADS performance but makes fair comparison with prior work difficult and complicates reproduction

Heavy dependence on visual pretraining inadequately discussed: CLIP-pretrained ViT-B used throughout; from-scratch ViT-B (A.4.3) shows significant drops; this privileged information contradicts 'action-free learning' framing but is relegated to appendix

Incomplete failure mode analysis: back-and-forth motions identified as problematic (Section 4.3) but no concrete examples from experiments, no systematic characterization of affected tasks, and no ablation evaluating the proposed observation history fix
Hyperparameter α requires task-specific tuning: while Appendix A.4.1 shows some robustness, adaptive selection is ad-hoc and unclear how sensitive this is for new domains

Limited mechanistic understanding: minimal interpretation of what features drive temporal distance predictions; unclear whether model captures temporal edges, velocities, semantic progress, or combinations thereof

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing practical challenge of reward engineering in robotics
Comprehensive experimental analysis structured around five research questions with multiple evaluation perspectives (VOC metric, representation learning, downstream RL)
Strong empirical results on Meta-World (9/10 tasks) and outperforming environment-provided dense rewards
Effective ablation studies demonstrating contribution of implicit negative sampling, weighted sampling, and discretization components
Cross-domain transfer capability demonstrated with human videos
Well-organized presentation with informative visualizations of learned representations
weaknesses: Theoretical justification in Section 4.3 acknowledges but does not adequately address fundamental limitations: assumes fully observable MDP, breaks down for visual aliasing and back-and-forth motions, and proposes observation history fix without experimental validation

Incremental technical contribution combining existing ideas (temporal structure from videos, self-supervised learning) with moderate engineering choices (temporal distance, two-hot discretization, weighted sampling P(Δ)∝1/Δ) that lack strong conceptual novelty compared to TCN/VIP/Rank2Reward/PROGRESSOR

Non-standard experimental setup using diverse initialization explicitly acknowledged to disadvantage OT/ADS baselines, but this critical detail is relegated to Appendix A.5.2 rather than prominent disclosure in main results section, raising fairness concerns
Misleading 'action-free' framing—method still requires binary success signals (privileged environmental information), substantially limiting practical applicability claims
Narrow evaluation scope limited to Meta-World manipulation tasks with similar structure; only 1 task in appendix for ManiSkill3; no evaluation on navigation, reasoning tasks, or diverse embodiments
Heavy dependence on CLIP-pretrained ViT-B backbone with significant performance degradation with from-scratch models (Figure 14), limiting practical advantage over manually designed rewards
Implicit negative sampling assumption (all backward movement is suboptimal) is not justified for tasks with multi-modal demonstrations or necessary backtracking
Missing critical experiment on tasks with back-and-forth motions to validate proposed observation history solution to identified POMDP limitation

strengths: Clear and intuitive core idea: temporal distance prediction naturally encodes task progress through potential-based reward shaping
Strong empirical results: achieves near-perfect success (9/10 tasks) with only 200k interactions, outperforms 8 baselines and environment-provided dense rewards
Comprehensive experimental validation: well-structured evaluation addressing five research questions with thorough ablations isolating each component's contribution
Sound technical design: implicit negative sampling handles bidirectional temporal reasoning, weighted pair sampling emphasizes fine-grained progress, two-hot discretization provides stability

Excellent representation learning: Figure 5 demonstrates that learned features capture smooth task progression across training, held-out, and agent trajectories, with clear separation of success vs. failure cases
High reproducibility standards: extensive hyperparameter details, visual backbone specifications, human video data visualization, clear experimental protocols, and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: theoretical justification assumes full observability (MDP) but practical deployment uses high-dimensional visual observations (POMDP); proposed solution of frame history concatenation is never experimentally validated

Heavy reliance on sparse success signals: Figure 16 shows dramatic performance collapse without sparse signals; this undermines the 'action-free learning' claim and suggests the method learns fine-grained refinement rather than the complete reward signal

Critical dependence on visual pretraining: Figure 14 shows severe degradation with from-scratch ViT-B; unclear how much improvement derives from the method versus the strong CLIP-pretrained backbone, limiting generalization claims

Limited evaluation scope: primarily Meta-World tabletop manipulation with only 3 of 10 tasks tested on human videos (20 videos per task); no evaluation on other manipulation benchmarks or real robot tasks; single ManiSkill3 task in appendix

Experimental setup choices need justification: deliberately diverse initializations chosen to disadvantage OT-based methods (A.5.2); goal-conditioned baselines provided with goal images while TimeRewarder doesn't—unequal comparison; weighted sampling distribution P(Δ)∝1/Δ lacks sensitivity analysis

Unvalidated solution to POMDP aliasing: paper acknowledges back-and-forth motions and visual aliasing cause issues and proposes frame history as solution, but never experimentally demonstrates this works
Missing computational analysis: no comparison of computational overhead, training time for reward model, or inference cost during RL—important for practical adoption and reproducibility

Underdeveloped cross-domain insights: Figure 7 shows human videos provide marginal benefit with 100 in-domain demos; main advantage only when severely data-starved; insufficient analysis of what visual properties transfer across domains
